name: Fat repositioning (tear trough)

lead: Fat repositioning softens under-eye bags and the tear trough hollow beneath them in one step, for a smoother, fresher lower lid. Rather than removing the bulging fat, as traditional lower blepharoplasty does, it relocates it.

Orbital fat that would otherwise form a bag is released and moved over the bony rim to fill the hollow below it. Published evidence consists of surgeon-reported case series of 66, 97 and 232 patients, covering transconjunctival repositioning, external fixation of the moved fat and whether visibly herniated fat is needed. No randomised trials were found in the sources reviewed.

paras: A surgeon performs it under anesthesia through an incision inside the lower lid or just under the lashes, sometimes securing the fat with fixation sutures. A canthopexy is sometimes added. The smoother lid contour shows after swelling settles.

Lower-eyelid surgery can cause eyelid malposition and other complications, and surgeons sometimes add a canthopexy to reduce that risk. Procedure-specific complication data were not summarised in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Under-eye fat is moved into the tear trough hollow rather than cut out, so the bag and the hollow smooth together for a fresher lower lid. The result is visible after healing. Support comes from surgeon case series rather than randomised trials.

lead: Fat repositioning is a lower-eyelid surgical technique in which the orbital fat that would otherwise bulge as an under-eye bag is released and moved over the infraorbital rim to fill the hollow beneath it, known as the tear trough [1][2]. People seek it for a smoother, less tired-looking transition between lower eyelid and cheek, using their own tissue and treating the bag and the hollow in one operation. It contrasts with traditional lower blepharoplasty, in which herniated fat is simply removed.

The literature on the technique is made up chiefly of surgeon-reported case series: a 66-patient series of transconjunctival repositioning in the sub-orbicularis oculi fat (intra-SOOF) plane published in 2006, a 232-patient series published in 2024 that reported tear trough deformity eliminated in over 85 percent of cases, and a 97-patient cohort of transcutaneous surgery published in 2025 that reported resolution in over 92 percent [3][4][5]. A randomised comparison of 40 patients was published in 2025 [6]. Review articles list fat transposition among the standard modern lower-blepharoplasty options for inferior orbital hollowing and the lid-cheek junction [2][7].

On looksmax.org, tear trough hollows are a recurring appearance concern, and fat repositioning is mentioned alongside hyaluronic acid filler and fat grafting as part of the menu of options for the under-eye area [8][9][10].

paras: In fat repositioning the orbital fat pads are released and redistributed along the infraorbital rim to smooth contour irregularities and treat tear trough deformity, rather than being excised [1]. Wikipedia places it within lower blepharoplasty, which may be done through an incision inside the lower lid (transconjunctival, leaving no external scar) or just below the lashes (transcutaneous, which allows skin removal as well) [1]. Surgeons may add procedures such as canthopexy or midface elevation to improve the transition from lower lid to cheek and to reduce the risk of eyelid malposition [1][2].

The tear trough is the groove where the lower eyelid meets the cheek. A bulging fat pad above the groove can accentuate the hollow beneath it. Moving fat from the bulge into the groove addresses both features with the person's own tissue [2]. Autologous fat grafting, in which fat is harvested elsewhere and injected, is a separate technique that adds volume rather than relocating what is already there [1].

sections.h: How people use it to improve their looks
paras: People who choose fat repositioning typically have a visible under-eye bag with a hollow immediately below it. The objective is a continuous, smooth contour from the lower lid to the cheek and a rested look, without foreign filler material. Looksmax.org posters who discuss tear trough hollows describe a hollow under the eye (one calls it a hereditary tear trough) and compare fat grafting, filler and surgery as routes to correct it [8][9][10].

A 97-patient study measured outcomes with the FACE-Q lower eyelid scales, which assess how people feel about the appearance of the lower lid area, and reported significant improvement in those scores and in social confidence [5].

A 2006 series in Ophthalmic Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery described transconjunctival repositioning with dissection in the intra-SOOF plane in 66 consecutive patients with a mean age of 56. Surgery was usually done in an office procedure room under local anaesthesia, patients were followed for about six months on average, and the authors rated outcomes and satisfaction as excellent with few complications or revisions [3].

subs.h: External fixation of the repositioned fat
paras: A 2025 study in Aesthetic Surgery Journal examined 97 patients operated on between May 2022 and December 2023 using percutaneous external fixation of the redistributed fat in transcutaneous blepharoplasty. The authors noted that internal fixation had been standard in the transcutaneous approach while external fixation had gained popularity in transconjunctival surgery. With a mean follow-up of 7.2 months, tear trough deformity and eyelid bags had resolved in over 92 percent of cases; satisfaction averaged 71.0 on a 100-point scale. Isolated patients needed revision for haematoma evacuation, fat injection, excess fat excision or skin excision [5].

A 2024 retrospective series in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery covered 232 patients, 198 primary and 34 who had previously had fat removed, all with minimal or no excess herniation. The authors challenged what they described as a strong belief that herniated fat is a prerequisite. Deformity was eliminated in over 85 percent, and the share of patients rated as having extremely or moderately severe deformity fell from 86.3 percent before surgery to 34.0 percent afterwards. A published discussion of the paper also exists [4][11].

A 2020 review in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology describes the transconjunctival route as suited to younger patients with prominent lower fat pad herniation and little excess skin, and the transcutaneous route to patients who also need skin excision. It notes that current practice goes beyond sculpting the three orbital fat pads to relocating intraorbital fat to correct inferior orbital hollowing and blend the lid-cheek junction [2]. A 2016 review lists fat transposition among techniques that also include fat excision, orbicularis suspension, lateral canthal tightening, malar suspension and skin resurfacing, matched to issues such as malar descent, tear trough deformity and lid laxity [7].

Wikipedia notes that transconjunctival surgery may need additional procedures when skin laxity is present, and that blepharoplasty overall is more commonly performed on women, who made up about 85 percent of US cases in 2014 [1].

Hyaluronic acid filler is a widely used non-surgical option, and a periorbital rejuvenation review says fillers can camouflage orbital fat pseudoherniation and tear trough deformity [12]. A systematic review of delayed complications after tear trough filler examined 52 patients from 28 articles; swelling (42.3 percent) and lumps or nodules (25 percent) were the most common, followed by xanthelasma-like reactions (17.3 percent) and migration (7.7 percent), with mean onset about 16.8 months after treatment [13].

Autologous fat grafting is another option. A 2025 prospective randomised study of 40 patients published in the Journal of Stomatology, Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery compared transconjunctival lower blepharoplasty with orbital fat repositioning against another approach for tear trough deformity; its abstract reports shorter operating time and better maintenance of results at follow-up for the modified technique, scored with the Barton and GAIS scales [6]. Some looksmax.org posters describe filler as causing swelling but no downtime, and others ask whether fat placed over weak bony support will sag with age [9][10].

Lower-eyelid surgery in general carries risks including eyelid malposition, which is why adjuncts such as canthopexy are used by some surgeons, and Wikipedia notes that swelling and bruising are common and usually settle over several weeks [1]. In the 232-patient series, undercorrection occurred in 30 patients, transient conjunctival bleeding in 12, dry eye in 6 and eyelid numbness in 2, all resolving spontaneously [4]. The 97-patient series reported isolated revisions for haematoma, fat injection or excision, and skin excision [5].

Published human studies are mainly surgeon-reported case series at Level IV evidence: 66 patients (2006), 232 patients (2024) and 97 patients (2025) [3][4][5]. The 2025 randomised study enrolled 40 patients between August 2020 and August 2022 [6]. A review of the lower blepharoplasty literature noted that much of it is lower-level evidence [2]. A registered trial on preserving the medial fat pad in upper eyelid blepharoplasty (n=50) concerns a related but different eyelid procedure [14].

The first-century Roman writer Celsus described excising eyelid skin, and the German surgeon Karl Ferdinand von Gräfe coined the term blepharoplasty in 1818 [1]. Lower-lid surgery moved over time from removing fat toward preserving and redistributing it, and the 2006 intra-SOOF series was described by its authors as a novel technique [3][1].

Tear trough hollows are a common concern on looksmax.org. Posters discuss fat grafting and filler as options, with one planning a fat graft and another reporting small filler volumes per side as giving immediate corrections [9][10]. Members also debate whether a bone-level cause limits what soft-tissue fixes can achieve, and one poster describes a hereditary hollow as a worry [8].
